`mcp 0.3` added support for more response families and link functions. For example, you can now do

```{r, eval=FALSE}
fit = mcp(model, data = df, family = gaussian("log"))
fit = mcp(model, data = df, family = binomial("identity"))
```


This is an ongoing effort and more will be added. This table shows the current status:

![](https://github.com/lindeloev/mcp/raw/docs/vignettes/_figures/mcp_glm_status.png)

 * **Green:** supported and the default priors are unlikely to change.
 * **Yellow:** supported but the default priors may change.
 * **White:** not currently supported. [Raise a GitHub issue](https://github.com/lindeloev/mcp/issues) if you need it.
 * **Red:** impossible or will not be supported.

See the "GLM" menu above for more details on using GLM with `mcp`.


# General remarks
Some link functions are *default* in GLMs for good reasons: they are computationally convenient and interpretable. A non-default link can imply impossible values, at which point `mcp` errors. For example, a `bernoulli("identity")` model `prob ~ 1 + x` places a slope directly on `P(y = TRUE)`, which can easily fall below 0 or exceed 1. Informative [priors](../articles/priors.html), for example through truncation, can prevent the sampler from visiting invalid values.

In short: think carefully and proceed at your own risk.


# An example

```{r}
library(mcp)
future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 3)
set.seed(42)  # Make the script deterministic
```


Reviving the example from the article on [binomial models in mcp](../articles/binomial.html)...

```{r}
model = list(
  y | trials(N) ~ 1 + x,  # Intercept and slope on success probability
  ~ 1 + x                 # Disjoined slope on success probability
)
```

we can model it using an `identity` link function:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
data = mcp_example_data("binomial")
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data = mcp_example_data("binomial")
fit = mcp(model, data = data, family = binomial(link = "identity"))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
message("Parallel sampling in progress...

Error in update.jags(model, n.iter, ...) : Error in node loglik_[63]
Invalid parent values")
```


Oops, the sampler visited impossible success probabilities, below 0 or above 1. For these data, the second-segment slope has too much posterior support for exceeding 1 under the defaults. We therefore use more informative priors that make a long, steep slope unlikely:

```{r, results=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
prior = list(
  x_2 = "dnorm(0, 0.002)",         # Slope is unlikely to be steep
  cp_1 = "dnorm(30, 10) T(20, )"   # Slope starts not-too-early
)

fit = mcp(model, data = data, family = binomial(link = "identity"), prior = prior, seed = 42)
```

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
set.seed(42)
plot(fit)
```

Sampling succeeded! This is a bad model of this data. But it illustrates the necessary considerations and steps to ameliorate problems when going beyond default link functions.

Because of the identity link, the binomial regression coefficients are intercepts and slopes on the success probability, in contrast to the log-odds fitted by `family = binomial(link = "logit")`. For example, `Intercept_1` is the success probability at `x = 0`, and `Intercept_2` is the success probability at `x = cp_1`.

```{r}
summary(fit)
```


# Specific remarks

 * The mean ($1 / {inverse\_link}(\lambda)$) is plotted for `family = exponential()` and output by `fit$simulate(..., fype = "fitted")`. Multiply by `log(2)` to get the median.

```{r cleanup, include=FALSE}
future::plan(future::sequential)
```
